transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-21 11:00am PT (15:00Z)
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Atlas CTO), Liam (Lead Eng), Jordan (PM)

Summary:
Avery opened with a short hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming behavior, generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop) and practical retry/backoff for production chat. Marcus demoed live code using Redwood SDK and showed a small benchmark comparing streaming vs non-streaming latency for short/long contexts. Customer asked about data residency, KMS, and how repeated partial responses are handled on reconnects. Call closed with next steps to provide pricing, benchmark artifacts and pilot scheduling.

Topics: streaming behavior, chunking/partial tokens, resume on reconnect, temperature/top_p effects, token accounting, retry/backoff patterns, SDK examples, security compliance links

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Avery: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, um quick intros and then we can jump right in. I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on this account, with Marcus our systems eng, he'll do the deep part.
[00:08] Priya: Hi, Priya here, we've got about half hour maybe 40 minutes, thanks.
[00:12] Marcus: Hey, good to meet you all. Quick note, I shared the quickstart gist in the chat — sorry the link is long — but it's the streaming example plus a small benchmark.
[00:25] Jordan: got it, thanks.

[00:30] Avery: Goal for today: show hosted API streaming basics, how params shape outputs, and what to do when streams drop — retries and graceful resume. Also show Console quick look and where Optimize suggestions live.

[01:05] Marcus: Ok I'll start with a tiny live run. I'm going to open Node example: call.redwood.com/v1/generate with stream=true. In the SDK we do redwood.chat.stream({model: 'rwd-open-7b', messages, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 256}) — note low temp for deterministic customer UX.
[01:30] Liam: Quick question — are you sending the whole convo each time or using prefix cache? We have long convo history.
[01:36] Marcus: Great Q. Hosted API supports prefix/KV cache on the runtime; for now we send the active window and use the platform's prefix caching for repeated system prompts. On Dedicated you can pin cache behavior. Sorry if I said K V cache earlier, the transcript might show KVS cache, but it's just KV.

[02:10] Marcus: Starting the stream — you'll see the SDK emits chunks as we go. Example: first chunk has partial token(s), like 'Hello, my name...' then more tokens append. Important: chunks are not sentence aligned, they are token stream.
[02:40] (audio drop, brief reconnect)
[02:50] Priya: We noticed some clients get partial sentences and then reconnect — how do you recommend handling duplicates?
[02:56] Marcus: Two common patterns: idempotent client merging and server-side event IDs. Our SDK emits token offsets and a final 'done' event. On reconnect, you can request from last acked offset or use model-level dedupe — but simpler approach is to buffer until 'done' then commit. For low-latency chat, we show incremental rendering and if reconnect happens, resume from last confirmed token sequence number.
[03:35] Jordan: Is there a cost implication for resumed streams?
[03:39] Avery: You pay per token consumed; resumed tokens count normally. We try to avoid double-billing on transient retries by providing a session id and offsets, but app-level dedupe also helps. Marcus: also note the Console shows token counts per session so you can audit.

[04:05] Marcus: Now let's try parameter influence — temperature 0.0 vs 0.8, top_p 1.0 vs 0.6. I'll run two quick examples: same prompt, different temps.
[04:25] (typing)
[04:35] Marcus: Temp 0.0 produced concise, repetitive phrasing — good for deterministic completions. Temp 0.7 gave more varied phrasing. For Atlas retail, where you want consistent product descriptions, low temp and prompt templates are usually better.

[05:10] Liam: We do both: product descriptions (deterministic) and customer-facing coaching suggestions (creative). Is it ok to use multiple models/endpoints?
[05:18] Avery: Yes, you can route by policy. Hosted supports multiple model catalog entries. Console lets you map routes by path and choose fallback variants.

[05:45] Marcus: On retries/backoff — recommended pattern: immediate short retry for transient network errors (exponential backoff jitter). For generation timeouts we recommend background re-try to a fallback model (smaller quantized variant) rather than full client retry. Example: client receives 504 after 20s; app should trigger a fallback path to rwd-open-3b-quant and surface a partial response to user with "still thinking" indicator.

[06:30] Priya: How do you handle long-running streaming calls and client WebSocket timeouts from mobile networks?
[06:38] Marcus: We advise a heartbeat and reconnect strategy. The streaming token offsets mean you can resume from last ack. Mobile networks: consider chunk-size and server-side small flush intervals so clients see tokens sooner and avoid idle timeouts. We also suggested reducing flush interval in the SDK config for mobile.

[07:20] (Marcus shares a small benchmark chart)
[07:25] Marcus: Here is our 50k token test: median token latency for streaming (small prompt) was ~50ms/token on hosted in us-west; non-streaming had a higher first-byte latency but similar overall cost. Note: exact numbers depend on model variant and batch windows.

[08:00] Jordan: Any memory/perf difference when using long context windows?
[08:05] Marcus: Yes, kv caching reduces compute for repeated prefixes but larger context increases memory and may change kernel selection. That's why our Optimize tool suggests quantization and batching settings by workload. For long contexts, you may want a model variant with longer context support and configure prefix cache to keep system prompts in cache.

[09:10] Priya: Security: we need SOC2, KMS integration, and audit logs for token access. Does hosted support customer-managed keys?
[09:20] Avery: Hosted supports encryption-at-rest and we offer KMS integration on Dedicated and Private; for hosted we have bring-your-own-key options in enterprise plans. Audit logs and per-token tracing are in Console (you can set retention). I'll attach our security one-pager.

[10:05] Liam: Do you have SSO for the Console?
[10:08] Avery: Yes SAML/SSO, RBAC, and SCIM provisioning.

[10:20] Marcus: Back to retries: code snippet (pseudocode) —
client.stream({onChunk(c){ ack(c.offset); render(c.text) }, onError(e){ if transient then retryWithBackoff(); else show fallback; }})

[10:50] Priya: When you retry with backoff, do you re-send the same prompt body? Concerned about duplication of tokens if not resumed properly.
[10:58] Marcus: We prefer resume with offset. If resume isn't possible, use an application-level dedupe token and check server-side — some customers implement a checksum on last committed tokens and skip duplicates.

[11:30] Jordan: Could you demo the Console where Optimize suggests batching tweaks?
[11:34] Avery: Yep — switching view. In Console > Optimize we have workload profiles, suggested batch_size, max_seq_len, quantization profile. I'll click the 'suggestions' for "chat - product-description" workload. It recommends lower batch_size for latency-sensitive flows and a different kernel for 8-bit quant.

[12:20] Marcus: We recommend you run a small pilot: route a single API route to a hosted model; capture token distributions for a week and then Redwood Optimize will propose config changes.

[12:45] (brief lag)
[12:50] Priya: For pilot, our infra team will need a checklist — network ports, allowlisted egress, IP ranges, and compliance docs.
[12:58] Avery: We'll provide an infra checklist and compliance pack. I'll send the list and the SOC2 artefact.

[13:20] Marcus: Last bit on streaming semantics: finalization events may be slightly delayed if model is waiting on stop tokens or penalty thresholds; always treat final done event as authoritative. Also if you request deterministic output, set temperature=0 and stop sequences.

[14:05] Liam: On concurrent requests — what's your guidance for per-route concurrency?
[14:10] Marcus: We expose concurrency controls and autoscale policies on Dedicated. For hosted, we have throttles per account; typical pattern: control concurrency client-side with token bucket and backpressure. Console shows per-route QPS and tail latency.

[14:50] Priya: Any gotchas if we mix hosted and dedicated?
[14:54] Avery: Routes can be routed by policy; fallback to hosted is possible. Ensure data egress rules match; Dedicated gives isolation guarantees. We'll document reference architectures.

[15:30] Jordan: Ok let's recap next steps.
[15:33] Avery: Recap: send pricing + compliance, Marcus sends benchmark and small README for the SDK streaming resume example, Priya to confirm pilot stakeholders. Team will reconvene after Atlas reviews.
[15:45] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[15:47] Avery: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Bye.

Notes on transcription imperfections: names sometimes hyphenated, occasional mis-hears (eg KVS -> KV store), code punctuation missing. The client asked for a 50k token benchmark and a pilot checklist.
